newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Serbian Socialists elaborate economic reforms.
newsitem.headline: Serbian Socialists elaborate economic reforms.

text.p: The ruling Socialist Party of Serbia (SPS), criticised for slow progress on reforms, reiterated on Friday its commitment to comprehensive economic reforms and highlighted a programme it hopes will create prosperity in Serbia.

"In January, the SPS decided to define 1997 as the year of reforms and afterwards we have established a council for economic reforms... as a body to lead the process, direct it, initiate and speed up changes," said Dusko Matkovic, president of the SPS Council for Economic Reforms.

"I want to stress there is an absolute political will in the SPS and commitment to implement reforms...and that the country should reintegrate with the world economy," Matkovic, also an SPS vice-president, told a news conference.

Economists at home and abroad have accused the SPS, led by President Slobodan Milosevic, of keeping a tight grip on the Serbian economy, which has been crippled by sanctions imposed during the war in Bosnia, and foot-dragging on reform.

But Matkovic said SPS reforms included changes in the fiscal, pension, health and education systems, streamlining the state administration, a social programme, reform of the banking system, liberalisation of trade laws, cooperation with international institutions and a long-term development strategy for Serbia and Yugoslavia.
"These are all steps we intend to take in 1997," he said.

"With reforms and their implementation in the months ahead, we shall attempt to win voters' confidence," said Milorad Vucelic, another vice-president of the SPS and managing director of the new Telekom Srbija company.

A 49 percent stake in Telekom Srbija was sold this month to Italian and Greek telecom companies for a total of 1.568 billion German marks ($909 million) but generally foreign investment in the rump Yugoslavia has been low.
Vucelic said Serbia's privatisation law was attractive for investors, in line with the SPS programme, and was fair and prevented any cheap sell-off of socially-owned property.

The law did not entirely give answers to the problems of big state monopolies, which will be privatised under a special government programme. But it tried to eliminate mistakes and learn from experience of other post-communist economies, Vucelic said.

Yugoslav deputy prime minister Danko Djunic insisted a programme of market reforms would help Yugoslavia to create a transparent market economy. Serbia is the dominant partner in what remains of the Yugoslav federation.

Djunic said the government had delayed adoption of a law on releasing more than $4 billion in frozen savings for September, since it relied on privatisation slated to begin on October 31. The frozen savings law was expected to speed up privatisation and intensify development of the local financial market.
The hard currency savings were frozen when Yugoslavia began to disintegrate in 1992.

The Yugoslav minister reponsible for relations with the International Monetary Fund, Nebojsa Maljkovic, said transparent reforms were not an isolated issue but closely linked to the country's return to international financial institutions.
"The privatisation law, frozen savings law and trade liberalisation are directly linked to Yugoslavia's getting closer to international financial institutions," he said.
He noted that a Yugoslav delegation would meet foreign creditors of the "London club" group next week. "We expect some progress at the meeting," he said.
Serbian Privatisation Minister Milan Beko said he saw foreign investment in Serbia exceeding one billion dollars both in 1997 and in 1998.

"Our task is to invest money in the best possible way, to develop infrastructure as the best motivation for other investments, to improve and harmonise our legal framework and provide firms with soft loans to revive production," Beko said.
-- Gordana Filipovic, Belgrade newsroom, +381 11 222 4254 ($ = 1.725 German Marks)
